title: Equator AI burst behavior and cost projections — July 2027
content:
Executive summary:

This note documents the benchmarking sessions we ran for Equator AI (search-and-assistant product) to characterize burst behavior, tail latency, and unit-cost under a Dedicated deployment profile. The customer’s key questions were: 1) how will short (1–5 minute) bursts to 2–3× baseline QPS affect p95/p99 latency, 2) what autoscale and batching settings minimize cost without exceeding a 400ms p95 target for single-turn generative requests, and 3) what fallback/quantization options are viable for extreme tail events.

High level findings (summary):
- Under a Dedicated pool sized for baseline QPS (80 reqs/s), short bursts to 160–240 reqs/s increased p95 by 1.6–2.8× and p99 by 2.4–4.6× depending on model variant and batching.
- Warm-state KV cache hit rate reduced median token compute by ~12% for the assistant prompts we used; however cache warmup takes ~30–90s after a cold period depending on prompt entropy.
- Autoscale reaction times (warm-up/concurrency ramp) are the dominant contributor to p99 during microbursts: our configured spot-burst policy added ~700–1200ms on average before new replicas were ready to serve heavy concurrency.
- Cost projections: with current pricing and the customer’s traffic profile, adding a conservative 30% headroom (reserve GPUs) increased monthly unit cost by ~18% but reduced p99 tail latency by ~48% during repeated burst patterns. Using a quantized 8-bit variant for tails (fallback) can reduce token compute cost by ~40% while keeping p95 < 400ms, but requires downstream quality validation.

Test setup and artifacts:
- Models tested: Equator-Large (FP16), Equator-Large-Q8 (int8-like quantized build), and Equator-Medium (smaller footprint).
- Environment: Redwood Dedicated pool (g4dn-style baseline equivalence), 6 GPUs in baseline pool, 2 additional warmable spare GPUs for bursts.
- Batching config: continuous batching enabled, max_batch_size=64, batching_latency_target_ms=6 (low-latency setting) and an alternate config with batching_latency_target_ms=25 (cost-optimized).
- Workloads: two suites — (A) synthetic uniform short prompts (10–40 tokens), and (B) production-sampled assistant traffic (avg 78 tokens, heavy prefix reuse for 18% of requests).
- Measurement windows: steady-state (30m), single microburst (90s ramp to peak then 3m decay), repeated microburst pattern (12 bursts over 60m).
- Key metrics collected: RPS, concurrency, GPU utilization, per-request latency (p50/p90/p95/p99), KV cache hit rate, batch sizes, tokens generated, and estimated token compute cost.

Detailed observations:
1) Burst-induced queuing and batching effects
- At low batching_latency_target (6ms): average batch size remained small (8–14 tokens per request equivalent) which reduced per-token latency but increased per-request overhead under high concurrency. During bursts, batching did not grow fast enough to absorb the concurrency which caused queueing at the runtime and raised p99.
- At relaxed batching_latency_target (25ms): batch sizes grew to 28–46, which improved GPU efficiency and reduced per-token cost by ~22% in steady-state, but increased median latency by ~60ms — acceptable in cost-sensitive flows but often violated the 400ms p95 target for the larger model.

2) Autoscale characteristics and recommendations
- The default scale-up policy (threshold-based on GPU util) triggers new replicas after sustained 70%+ utilization for 30s; when bursts are sudden, that 30s window produces a significant latency penalty.
- Recommendation: use a hybrid policy — maintain 20–30% spare capacity during business hours (predictable bursts) plus a fast reactive policy that pre-warms up to 2 replicas based on a short-lived trajectory detector (5–10s). This reduces p99 by ~35–50% in our replayed burst patterns.

3) Cache behavior and prompt structure
- Prefix/KV cache gives highest benefit when the workload has high prefix reuse (we saw 18% reuse in production sample); cache hit yields ~12% lower compute and 8–12% lower latency on median.
- Cache warmup cost during cold periods: first 60–90s after idle shows elevated GPU usage as KV caches are rebuilt; recommend a short-lived keepwarm policy for latency-sensitive routes.

4) Fallback quantized variants for tails
- Equator-Large-Q8: in our conversational eval set, p95 remained within 10–18% of FP16 p95 for short answers, but quality drift appeared on long-form contextual completions. For search/snippet tasks it was indistinguishable.
- Operational pattern: route critical low-latency single-shot requests to Q8 if the serving pipeline detects queueing beyond threshold or if scale-up time is expected; route longer-context or high-quality requests to FP16.

Cost projection examples (monthly, USD) for customer traffic profile (baseline = 80 reqs/s avg, bursts to 200 reqs/s for cumulative 25% of traffic minutes):
- Baseline Dedicated, no spare: $92k/month (high p99 during bursts)
- Baseline + 30% reserved spare GPUs: $109k/month (+18%), p99 reduced by 48% in burst windows
- Baseline + fast pre-warm (no reserved but faster policy) + Q8 fallback: $99k/month (+7.6%), p99 reduced by 32% and net quality risk localized to tail routes
Notes: estimates include model token compute, GPU time amortization, and average batching improvements observed in our lab. Exact numbers will vary by region and instance SKU.

Operational playbook (recommended immediate steps):
- Short term (1–2 weeks):
  - Deploy Q8 variant behind a feature-flagged fallback for tail events, run A/B on a small % of traffic to validate quality.
  - Configure keep-warm for critical routes (30–90s TTL) and increase baseline pool by 20% during business hours.
  - Lower batching_latency_target on ultra-low-latency routes; use higher target for cost-sensitive batch routes.
- Medium term (1–2 months):
  - Implement trajectory-based scale detector (5–10s) to pre-warm replicas when a burst is predicted from short-term traffic trends.
  - Add route-level routing policies: prefer Q8 for short single-shot responses and FP16 for multi-turn.
- Long term (quarterly):
  - Jointly evaluate model distillation to produce a medium-size model that provides quality comparable to Equator-Large for common prompt classes; this reduces the need for frequent fallback.

Risks and open questions:
- Quality drift on Q8 for long-context completions — customer must define strict evaluation set for acceptable thresholds.
- Regional SKU availability could change cost calculus (we used region-us-west-2 equivalence).
- Autoscale changes require ops coordination and may interact with other tenants on the Dedicated pool if shared.

Appendix: selected raw metrics (single repeated microburst session sample)
- Baseline pool: 6 GPUs, spare: 2 warmable
- Peak RPS (burst): 210 req/s
- Median tokens generated per request: 78
- KV cache hit (production-sample): 18%
- Equator-Large FP16: p50=95ms, p90=210ms, p95=360ms, p99=920ms (during burst)
- Equator-Large-Q8: p50=110ms, p90=235ms, p95=410ms, p99=1100ms (during burst)
- Equator-Medium FP16: p50=72ms, p90=165ms, p95=220ms, p99=610ms
- Average GPU utilization during burst (baseline-only): 86–95%
- Average batch size (latency_target=6ms): 9–12
- Average batch size (latency_target=25ms): 32–44

Representative configuration snippets (for engineering handoff):
- Keep-warm: route=assistant-critical, keep_warm_ttl=60s, min_replicas=2
- Hybrid autoscale: baseline_min_replicas=6, reserve_headroom=30%, prewarm_detector_window=8s, prewarm_replicas=2
- Batching: continuous_batching=true, max_batch_size=64, batching_latency_target_ms=6 (low-latency) / 25 (cost-optimized)

Next steps for SE engagement:
- Validate Q8 fallback quality on the customer’s 200-case evaluation set (SE to coordinate with Equator ML team).
- Run a regionally-distributed replay for the next 72h with proposed autoscale changes to confirm p99 trends.
- Customer decision: accept +30% reserved headroom for guaranteed p99 improvement, or adopt dynamic prewarm+Q8 fallback for smaller cost increase but slightly higher quality risk on tails.
